papers.version_note: arXiv:2405.14072v2, 3 May 2025. The text layer carries the paper once, with figures reduced to axis labels and equations partly garbled; the last page break leaves an empty final segment.
papers.what_it_is: A paper that proposes quantum circuit Markov random fields, a problem-informed quantum circuit Born machine Ansatz built from the clique structure of a Markov network, with a benchmark construction, simulations against QCIBM, BBQC and a classical BN, a cost-variance trainability study and a conjecture of quantum advantage in sampling.

existing.value: The authors report that for the 10-node graphs the QCIBM model has 85 parameters, while the QCMRF circuits have 60, 58 and 66.
quotes: For these 10-node graphs, the corresponding QCIBM model has 85 parameters, while the QCMRF circuits only have 60, 58 and 66 respectively.
existing.certainty_reason: The paper states the parameter counts of the circuits it built for the random community graphs.

existing.value: The authors report that on the three 10-node random graphs with dense communities, their QCMRF models reach better performance than the problem-agnostic QCIBMs while significantly reducing the number of trainable parameters; the experiments use 5 sets of uniformly random factor values.

We consider 5 sets of uniformly random factor values and take the average performance over these.

existing.note: The conjecture rests on the stated assumption that the trained model reaches sufficient precision; see the new assertions on the argument and its basis.
existing.value: The authors state an informal conjecture that the QCMRF circuit class contains classically hard cases and so yields a quantum advantage in sampling; they do not prove it.
quotes: Informal Conjecture. The class of QCMRF circuits, that can learn probability distributions efficiently represented by MNs, also contains classically hard cases, yielding a quantum advantage in sampling.
existing.certainty_reason: The authors' own conjecture, built on cited hardness results for 1-level QAOA; not proved or tested in the paper.

assertions.value: The paper defines Problem 1 (Distribution Learning in MNs): given the graph structure and the clique factorization of a Markov network H with unknown joint distribution P*, a dataset D sampled from P*, and epsilon and delta in (0, 1), output with probability at least 1 - delta a representation of a distribution PM satisfying d(P*, PM) <= epsilon.
quotes: graph structure and the clique factorization of a Markov

network H with an unknown joint probability distribution P ∗, a dataset D sampled from P ∗ and ε, δ ∈ (0, 1), output with probability at least 1 − δ a representation of a distribution PM satisfying d(P ∗, PM) ≤ ε.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the learning problem it addresses as a numbered problem.

assertions.value: The authors propose a QCBM Ansatz for distribution learning in MNs: a parametrized many-body Ising Hamiltonian built from the clique structure of the MN, whose terms commute and are reparametrized so each term appears once with a distinct coefficient, with the generated unitary followed by the QCIBM-style final general one-qubit gates; they call these models quantum circuit Markov random fields (QCMRFs).
assertions.anchor: Section III A, p.6 and Appendix A, p.11-12
quotes: We propose a QCBM Ansatz for distribution learning in MNs, as described in Prob. 1.
Since all terms commute, we can reparametrize the Hamiltonian such that each term only appears once with a distinct coefficient (and identities are excluded)
QCBM models quantum circuit Markov random fields (QCMRFs).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its own model in Section III A.

assertions.value: The authors state that for pairwise MNs the QCMRF circuits have less or equal parameters than the corresponding QCIBM Ansatz, with equality only for complete graphs; they give the 2-local QCIBM parameter count as n(n-1)/2 + 4n, which is O(n squared), and say that with constant clique sizes the QCMRF parameter count is O(n).
quotes: Ansatz, this number is kQCIBM = n(n−1)/2+4n, which is O(n2).
These give rise to QCMRF circuits with less or equal
Ansatz, where we have equality only for complete graphs.
of nodes, the parameter count is O(n).
assertions.certainty_reason: Counting statement derived in the appendix; the QCMRF O(n) claim assumes constant clique sizes. The exponents are printed flat in the text layer.
assertions.reader_inference: The O(n) statement is conditional on a bounded clique size, which the paper states only in the preceding lines.

assertions.value: The authors state that converting a BN and an MN can introduce additional edges and so additional parameters, that BBQCs usually have more parameters than QCMRFs when the problem is defined by an MN, and that for chordal MNs with maximal clique factorization the number of parameters in the two model classes is equal.
quotes: Since the conversion between BNs and MNs can introduce additional edges, this conversion can also introduce additional parameters.
However, for chordal MNs, having maximal clique factorization, the number of parameters in the two model classes is equal.
assertions.certainty_reason: Counting argument in the appendix, stated in prose without a worked proof.

assertions.value: The authors state that the QCIBM needs no ancillas and so has n qubits, while QCMRF circuits can use no ancillas or nC ancillas, where nC is the number of cliques larger than 2, giving n + nC qubits.
quotes: For the QCIBM models, since they only contain
no ancillas leading to the same number, or we can use nC ancillas, where nC refers to the number of cliques, that are larger than 2.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the resources of the circuits as it builds them.

assertions.value: The authors state that a k-local MultiRZ gate can be implemented in linear depth with 2k CNOT gates and a single-qubit RZ rotation, and that one clique can use an ancillary qubit to need significantly fewer CNOT gates, adding an ancillary qubit for each clique of size > 2.
quotes: A k-local M ultiRZ gate can be implemented in linear depth with 2k CN OT gates and a single-qubit RZ rotation.
This approach reduces the number of gates and the depth, while adding an ancillary qubit for each clique of size > 2.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own circuit implementation.

assertions.value: The authors propose a benchmark in which, given an undirected graph, a set of cliques and a classical (pseudo)random number generator, each clique gets a factor table of 2 to the power |C| numbers drawn from the generator, the unnormalized measures are the products of table entries, these are normalized by the partition function, and the result is sampled classically to build the training set.
quotes: 1. To each clique C ∈ CH, we assign a factor as a set of 2|C| numbers obtained by querying the classical generator 2|C| times.
2. Next, we calculate the unnormalized measures of each global assignment by multiplying the corresponding element of each factor table.
3. To get the probability of each assignment, we then normalize the measures by the partition function.
4. Finally, we sample this joint probability distribution classically several times to construct the training dataset D.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its benchmark construction step by step.

assertions.value: The authors state that the difficulty of the learning problem is proportional to the clique sizes of the MN, that complexity can be raised by adding edges and taking maximal cliques of the new graph, and that in their experiments the factor values are sampled uniformly at random in an IID fashion from a positive range of real numbers.
quotes: In general, the “difficulty” of the learning problem is proportional to the clique sizes of the MN.
we sample these values uniformly at random in an IID fashion from a positive range of real numbers.
we can increase the complexity of the corresponding target distribution by introducing additional edges and considering the maximal cliques of the new graph.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the scope and setup of its benchmark; the proportionality is stated without a measurement.
assertions.reader_inference: The statement that difficulty is proportional to clique size is asserted, not measured as such; the grid experiments are the only related evidence.

assertions.value: The authors report that all experiments use the KL divergence and the MMD loss (the kernel being the average of 3 Gaussian kernels with sigma in {0.25, 10, 10 cubed}), Pennylane simulations, the Adam optimizer with learning rate 0.1, and 500 epochs; the KL loss has access to the exact target distribution while the MMD loss only accesses a finite training set.
quotes: the kernel function is calculated as the average of 3 different Gaussian kernels with σ ∈ {0.25, 10, 103}.
The KL divergence has access to the exact target probability distribution, while the MMD loss can only access a finite training set.
optimized with Adam [52], with learning rate 0.1. We train all models for 500 epochs.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its experimental setup.

assertions.value: The authors state that the TV distance between model and target is calculated analytically at each step, that the average performance over multiple random factor values is reported, and that curves are averaged over a window of 20 training epochs for visualization.
quotes: the TV distance between the model and target distributions is calculated analytically in each step.
For better visualization, we also average over a window of 20 training epochs.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states how it evaluates its results.

assertions.value: The authors report that in the grid-topology benchmarks against the QCIBM the number of training samples for the MMD loss and the number of quantum circuit evaluations were set to 104 (an exponent printed flat, read here as ten to the fourth power), with 5 sets of uniformly random factor values averaged, and the QCIBM has all-to-all connectivity.
quotes: The number of training samples for the MMD loss along with the number of quantum circuit evaluations was set to 104.
We consider 5 sets of uniformly random factor values and take the average performance over these.
problem-agnostic QCIBM with all-to-all connectivity

assertions.value: The authors state that all parameters of both models are initialized to 0 so that training starts in the equal superposition of all basis states, and say this strategy proved better than random initialization; no comparison is shown in the text.
quotes: All parameters of both models are initialized to 0, as in this setting, the model starts the training in the equal superposition of all basis states.
This strategy proved to be better than random initialization.

assertions.reader_inference: Setup part (zero initialization) is a stated setup; the comparison to random initialization is reported without a figure or table.

assertions.value: The authors report that on a 3 x 3 grid, which defines a pairwise MN, both models have similar performance while the QCMRF model reduces the number of trainable parameters from 72 to 48.

quotes: We start with a 3 × 3 grid, which defines a pairwise MN
Here, both models have similar performance, while our QCMRF model reduces the number of trainable parameters from 72 to 48.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one small simulated study.

assertions.value: The authors report that for the grid with added edges whose maximal cliques have size 3 the QCMRF shows some separation in performance with 60 parameters, and that for cliques of size 4 the QCMRF has 76 parameters and significantly outperforms the 2-local QCIBM.
assertions.anchor: Section III C 1, p.7 and Fig. 4 top row, p.8
quotes: All the maximal cliques of the second graph have size 3, leading to a 3-local Hamiltonian, that can capture higher-order correlations.
Here we can already see some separation in the performance, while still having less parameters (60) than the QCIBM.
In the last case, the cliques are of size 4, which increases the number of trainable parameters in the QCMRF circuit to 76.
In this case, our model significantly outperforms the 2-local QCIBM.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one small simulated study.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper compares against a 2-local QCIBM only; a QCIBM with higher-order terms is not tested.

assertions.value: The authors state that as graph connectivity and maximal clique size grow the distribution becomes harder to learn for the problem-agnostic QCIBM, while the QCMRF performance is either unaffected or even better, and conclude that higher-order Hamiltonians can help capture higher-order correlations.
quotes: This series of experiments show, that as we increase the connectivity of the graph and the sizes of its maximal cliques, the distribution becomes harder to learn, as it is reflected in the performance of the problem-agnostic QCIBM.
However, the performance of our problem-specific QCMRF model is either unaffected by this change, or it performs even better, as its complexity also increases with the underlying MN.
assertions.certainty_reason: An interpretation of three small grid experiments by the authors.
assertions.reader_inference: The text says the series 'proves' the point; three instances with 5 factor draws are suggestive, not a proof.

assertions.value: The authors report that on the third random community graph, where the communities are connected by a node with large centrality measures, the QCMRF model significantly outperforms the problem-agnostic case.
assertions.anchor: Section III C 1, p.7 and Fig. 4 bottom row, p.8
quotes: Furthermore, in the third graph, where the communities are connected by a node with large centrality measures, the QCMRF model significantly outperforms the problem-agnostic case.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one small simulated study.

here we started with random values to have a more fair comparison.

assertions.value: The authors report that on loop graphs the QCMRF models reach similar performance to BBQCs while having a much lower cost of implementation; the triangulation needed for the BBQC introduces n - 3 new edges and so increases the parameters and circuit depth.
assertions.anchor: Section III C 2, p.8-9 and Fig. 5
quotes: the triangulation introduces n−3 new edges.
In all cases, our MN-based model reaches similar performance to BBQCs, while having much lower cost of implementation

assertions.reader_inference: Loop graphs are non-chordal, the case favorable to QCMRF; the paper itself says BBQCs do better on chordal graphs.

assertions.value: The authors remark that BBQCs show better performance on chordal graphs, where both PGM-based models have the same number of trainable parameters, and that BN-based models are therefore better at capturing the target distribution there although requiring much deeper circuits.
quotes: BBQCs show better performance on chordal graphs, where both PGM-based models have the same number of trainable parameters.
This means, that for chordal graphs, BN-based models are better at capturing the target distribution, although requiring much deeper circuits.
assertions.certainty_reason: A limitation stated in the conclusion with no data shown for it in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors report, from exact-simulation KL training on triangle chain graphs (3-gram models, cliques of size 3) averaged over 5 independent problems, that the performance separation between QCMRF and QCIBM is independent of the problem size, and that for 20 qubits the parameter counts are 135 and 270 respectively.
quotes: The separation in the average performance between the QCMRF and QCIBM models is independent of
the problem size, while the number of parameters is O(n) and O(n2) respectively. For 20 qubits, this amounts to 135 and 270 parameters.
We show the average of 5 independent problems, having different sets of factor values.
For this comparison, we use the triangle chain graph, that is equivalent to the 3-gram model, as in Eq. (C3), each clique being of size 3.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study; the qubit range 10 to 20 is read from Fig. 10 and 11.
assertions.reader_inference: The QCIBM figure of 270 matches n(n-1)/2 + 4n at n = 20. The training is KL on exact probabilities, which the paper calls not realistic.

assertions.value: The authors state that the exact-simulation experiments use only the KL divergence on exact model and target probabilities, that this training is not realistic, and that it allows scaling to larger problems than the main text.
quotes: While this training is not realistic, as it requires the exact probabilities from both distributions, this way, the simulation can be scaled up to larger problems, than the ones considered in the main text.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the limit of its own exact-simulation setup.

assertions.value: The authors report, on the 9-node grid MN turned into a BN and fitted by maximum likelihood with pgmpy, that the QCMRF model shows similar performance with small training sets (100, 500 and 1000 samples were tried) but weaker performance when the number of samples is increased.
quotes: While our model shows similar performance with small training sets, its performance is weaker when the number of samples is increased.
We consider the grid graph topology with 9 nodes, and turn the corresponding MN into a BN.
We repeat this procedure for 100, 500 and 1000 training samples.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one small study; a limitation the authors state.
assertions.reader_inference: This is the only comparison to a classical model, and the classical model is better at larger sample sizes.

assertions.value: The authors state that the weaker performance against classical methods highlights the need for more enhanced training methods for quantum models, but does not affect the potential of the model for quantum advantage in sampling, since these classical methods are known to be unscalable.
quotes: This highlights the need for more enhanced training methods for quantum models, however, this does not affect the potential of our model to have quantum advantage in sampling the learned probability distribution, since these classical methods are known to be unscalable.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own argument, with no support in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The classical model compared is a maximum-likelihood BN on a 9-node grid; the scalability statement is not shown or cited there.

we define 10 sets of uniformly random factor values and in each case, we evaluate the variance using 104 sets of random circuit parameters.

analyse the depth accordingly. We also assume full con-

assertions.value: The paper argues in Appendix A that, because the entangling gates in UZ commute and the light-cone of Zi contains only neighbours of node i, the Markov property holds for all output variables, and by the Hammersley-Clifford theorem the output distribution of QCMRF circuits factorizes according to the same MN structure, assuming positive probabilities.
quotes: Therefore, the Markov property applies to all output random variables simultaneously.
Consequently, the output probability distribution of QCMRF circuits factorizes according to the same MN structure, assuming positive probabilities.
assertions.certainty_reason: An informal argument in the appendix rather than a stated theorem, resting on a cited result (Hammersley-Clifford).
assertions.reader_inference: The light-cone step is argued in prose; it is not given as a numbered lemma, and the condition of positive probabilities is stated only at the end.

assertions.value: The authors state that the factors are not normalized in general, so the joint distribution need not equal the product of the clique marginals, and that they expect the independent trainable final one-qubit gates to give enough flexibility to compensate for this mismatch.
quotes: However, since the factors are not normalized in general, the joint distribution is not necessarily the same as the factor product of the marginal ones.
We expect, that this expressivity enhancement provides enough flexibility to compensate for the mismatch coming from the different scale of the marginal distributions.
assertions.certainty_reason: An expectation stated by the authors, not proved.

assertions.value: The paper defines quantum learning advantage (Definition 5) as the existence of a class of distributions that is (d, epsilon, k, BQP)-learnable but not (d, epsilon, k, BPP)-learnable, and quantum advantage in sampling (Definition 6) as a quantum algorithm A1 in BQP that can efficiently sample PM1 within epsilon of P while no classical algorithm A2 in BPP can sample some PM2 within epsilon of P efficiently.
assertions.anchor: Definitions 5 and 6, Section III E, p.10
quotes: Definition 6 (Quantum Advantage in Sampling).
Definition 5 (Quantum Learning Advantage). An algorithm A ∈ BQP is said to have quantum learning advantage, if there exists a class of distributions P n for which there exists d, ϵ, k such that
P n is (d, ε, k, BQP )learnable, but not (d, ε, k, BP P )-learnable, where this concept of learnability is defined in Def. 4.

a quantum algorithm A1 ∈ BQP is said to have quantum advantage in sampling from the distribution P , if A1 can efficiently sample PM1 and no classical algorithm A2 ∈ BP P can sample PM2 efficiently, where d(P, PM2) ≤ ε.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the definitions.

assertions.value: The paper defines a class of distributions as (d, epsilon, k, C)-learnable if some algorithm in complexity class C, given delta and a dataset of size k from any P in the class, outputs with probability at least 1 - delta a representation of PM with d(P, PM) <= epsilon, running in time poly(1/epsilon, 1/delta, n); it says it extended the definition from Ref. [13] with sample complexity.
quotes: Definition 4 ((d, ε, k, C)-learnable). For a metric d, ϵ > 0, k > 0 and complexity class C,
A should run in time poly(1/ε, 1/δ, n).
With this, we extended the definition from [13] with the sample complexity
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the definition.

assertions.value: The authors state that their argument assumes the joint distribution of a target MN is learnable by both an arbitrary classical model and a QCMRF model to a given precision epsilon, that it concerns advantage in sampling (the second definition), and that it rests on the claim that the QCMRF class contains the QAOA and IQP circuits.
quotes: we concentrate on this second definition and argue, that since our QCMRF model class contains the class of QAOA and IQP circuits, it can also produce distributions that are thought to be classically hard.
we assume, that the joint distribution of a target MN is learnable by both an arbitrary classical model and a QCMRF model to a given precision ε
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' stated assumptions for an argument, with the containment claim not proved in the text.
assertions.reader_inference: Containment of QAOA/IQP in the QCMRF class is asserted; the text does not show the construction, and the final measurement basis and the mixer layer differ.

assertions.value: The authors state that Ref. [7] proved that efficient classical sampling of the output distribution of the 1-level QAOA circuit implies the collapse of the polynomial hierarchy to the third level, shown for multiplicative error only.
quotes: In [7], the authors proved, that efficient classical sampling of the output distribution of the 1-level QAOA circuit implies the collapse of the polynomial hierarchy to the third level.
On the other hand, this was shown for multiplicative error only
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to Ref. [7].

assertions.value: The authors state that Ref. [57] extended the multiplicative-error results from worst case to average case hardness for 1-level QAOA circuits, and that in Ref. [38] the author proved average case hardness with additive error, which they call the strongest result known to them for weak simulation of 1-level QAOA circuits.
quotes: These results using multiplicative error were extended in Ref. [57] from worst case to average case hardness for 1-level QAOA circuits.

Finally, in Ref. [38], the author proved average case hardness with additive error, which, up to our knowledge, is the strongest result in connection with the weak simulation of 1-level QAOA circuits.
assertions.certainty_reason: Results the paper attributes to Refs. [57] and [38].

assertions.value: The authors state that their framework mostly concerns distance measured in TV, which is equivalent to additive error, and that multiplicative error is a stronger constraint, so that simulating up to a bounded additive error is a harder task.
quotes: In our framework, however, we mostly concentrated on distance as measured in TV, which is equivalent to additive error. Multiplicative error is a stronger constraint, thus simulating up to a bounded additive error is a harder task.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement by the authors, with no proof in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The relation between hardness under multiplicative and additive error is stated as a remark; the hardness claims that matter for the conjecture are cited, not derived here.

assertions.value: The authors state that, provided a QCMRF model can be trained to sufficient precision, the trained model can be used to efficiently sample the distribution of the underlying MN, and that the larger class containing 1-level QAOA circuits can also be hard to weakly simulate classically.
quotes: Since the class of probability distributions defined by the output of QCMRF circuits contains the 1level QAOA circuits, this larger class can also be hard to weakly simulate, i.e., to sample the output probability distribution efficiently classically.
This also means, that - provided that we can train a QCMRF model to sufficient precision - we can use the trained model to efficiently sample the distribution of the underlying MN.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' conditional argument; the condition (training to sufficient precision) is not shown to hold.
assertions.reader_inference: Hardness is cited for the circuit family, not shown for a distribution learned from a target MN; the main-text and classical-comparison results show a classical BN doing better with more samples.

assertions.value: The authors state in the conclusion that they presented an argument in the sampling setting, highlighting the potential of the model to improve over classical methods since it contains the class of QAOA circuits that are known to be hard to sample classically.
quotes: We presented an argument in the second setting, highlighting the potential of our model to offer improvements over classical methods, since it contains the class of QAOA circuits, that are known to be hard to sample classically.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' conclusion, resting on cited hardness results and the conjecture.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that their numerical experiments demonstrated that the QCMRF model can capture higher-order correlations between the binary random variables of the MN, which can significantly improve performance for higher-order target models, while potentially reducing the number of trainable parameters on sparse graphs compared to problem-agnostic approaches.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that the QCMRF models reached the performance of BBQCs on small loop graphs with fewer parameters and significantly shallower circuits.
quotes: The QCMRF models reached the performance of BBQCs on small loop-graphs with fewer parameters and significantly shallower circuits.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' conclusion from the loop-graph experiment.

assertions.value: The authors state that a major setback of their framework is that it assumes knowledge of the graph structure along with its cliques, while saying this knowledge is readily available in various use cases and that the approach can be used with classical structure learning algorithms.
quotes: Finally, what can be seen as a major setback of our framework is that it assumes knowledge of the graph structure along with its cliques.
While this seems like a major obstacle, this knowledge is readily available in various use cases.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states a limit of its own framework.

assertions.value: The authors state that learning a target distribution to high accuracy alone does not characterize generative model performance, that the model's ability to generalize rather than memorize was not assessed, and that this could be investigated with a limited-size training set.
quotes: While we concentrated on learning a target distribution to high accuracy, this alone is not enough to characterize the performance of generative models.
Another important factor is the model’s ability to generalize, rather than memorize the training data [58].
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states a limit of its own evaluation.

assertions.value: The authors list as possible extensions replacing the final general one-qubit unitaries with one-parameter rotations (e.g., RX rotations) and using multiple layers to resemble QAOA circuits more and reach the overparametrized regime; the model studied has a single UZ layer.
quotes: Possible extensions of our QCMRF model could include replacing the final set of general one-qubit unitaries Uf (Γ, ∆, Σ) with one-parameter rotations (e.g., RX rotations)
using multiple layers to have higher resemblance to QAOA circuits and to reach the overparametrized regime.
assertions.certainty_reason: Future work stated by the authors; the single-layer reading is inferred from the extension list.
assertions.reader_inference: Because the studied model has one UZ layer and general final gates, the 'contains QAOA' claim is not an identical-circuit statement.

assertions.value: The authors state that the KL divergence is unsuitable for data-driven training because it requires a large number of training samples, and that it was shown not to be trainable for larger-scale QCBMs (citing Ref. [43]).
quotes: Unfortunately, this function is also unsuitable for data-driven training, as it requires a large number of training samples, and it was shown not to be trainable for larger-scale QCBMs [43].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to Ref. [43].

assertions.value: The authors state that MN parameter estimation with complete data cannot in general be solved in closed form, that the objective is convex so iterative methods are guaranteed to converge, and that inference in MNs, needed at each gradient step, is #P-complete in general, making distribution learning fairly expensive or even intractable classically.

assertions.value: The authors state that the approach of Ref. [48] to sampling MNs on a quantum computer uses a polynomial approximation and real part extraction that can fail, so the success probability decreases exponentially with the number of maximal cliques.
